subject: science
chapter_title: The Amazing World of Solutes, Solvents, and Solutions

concepts.title: Solutions and Their Components
concepts.definition: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of two or more substances in which the solute is the substance that dissolves and the solvent is the substance that does the dissolving.
concepts.key_idea: Every solution has a solute (dissolved substance) and a solvent (dissolving medium); together they form a uniform single-phase mixture.
question_patterns: What is a solution? Define solute and solvent with an example.
Identify the solute and solvent in a sugar-water solution.
Why is a solution called a homogeneous mixture?
Give two everyday examples of solutions and name their components.
Can a solid be a solvent? Explain with an example.

solution_steps.explain: Examine the given mixture and check whether its components are uniformly distributed and cannot be distinguished by the naked eye.
Determine which substance is present in smaller amount and dissolves (solute) and which is present in larger amount and acts as the dissolving medium (solvent).
Confirm that the mixture is uniform throughout with no visible boundaries between solute and solvent, which qualifies it as a solution.

worked_examples.question: In a salt-water solution, which is the solute and which is the solvent?
worked_examples.solution: Salt is the substance that dissolves, so it is the solute. Water is the dissolving medium present in larger amount, so it is the solvent.

worked_examples.question: A tincture of iodine contains iodine dissolved in alcohol. Identify the solute and solvent.
worked_examples.solution: Iodine is the dissolved substance (solute) and alcohol is the dissolving medium (solvent).

exercises.question: Define solute and solvent. Give one example each.
Classify the following as solute or solvent: (a) oxygen in air, (b) water in sea water.

concepts.title: Types of Solutions
concepts.definition: Solutions can be classified based on the physical state of the solute and solvent as solid-liquid, liquid-liquid, or gas-liquid solutions, among others.
concepts.key_idea: The state (solid, liquid, gas) of the solute and solvent determines the type of solution; common types include solid in liquid, liquid in liquid, and gas in liquid.
question_patterns: Classify a solution as solid-liquid, liquid-liquid, or gas-liquid.
Give an example of a gas dissolved in a liquid.
What type of solution is an alloy? Justify your answer.
How is a liquid-liquid solution different from a solid-liquid solution?
List one example each of solid-solid and gas-gas solutions.

solution_steps.action: Determine the state of the solute
solution_steps.explain: Identify whether the dissolved substance is a solid, liquid, or gas under the given conditions.

solution_steps.action: Determine the state of the solvent
solution_steps.explain: Identify whether the dissolving medium is a solid, liquid, or gas.
Combine the two states (solute-solvent) to label the solution type, e.g., solid-liquid, liquid-liquid, or gas-liquid.

worked_examples.question: What type of solution is soda water (carbon dioxide dissolved in water)?
worked_examples.solution: Carbon dioxide is a gas (solute) and water is a liquid (solvent), so it is a gas-liquid solution.

worked_examples.question: Classify the solution formed when sugar is dissolved in water.
worked_examples.solution: Sugar is a solid solute and water is a liquid solvent, making it a solid-liquid solution.

exercises.question: Give one example each of a solid-liquid, liquid-liquid, and gas-liquid solution.
Vinegar is a solution of acetic acid in water. What type of solution is it?

concepts.title: Solubility and Factors Affecting It
concepts.definition: Solubility is the maximum amount of a solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at a particular temperature to form a saturated solution.
concepts.formula: solubility = (mass of solute / mass of solvent) x 100
concepts.key_idea: Solubility depends mainly on temperature and the nature of the solute and solvent; for most solids in water, solubility increases with temperature, while for gases it decreases with temperature.
question_patterns: Define solubility and state its units.
How does temperature affect the solubility of a solid in a liquid?
Why does a warm fizzy drink go flat faster than a cold one?
What effect does stirring have on the rate of dissolving?
Calculate the solubility if 36 g of salt dissolves in 100 g of water at a given temperature.

solution_steps.explain: Note the mass of the solute that dissolves and the mass of the solvent at the stated temperature.
Solubility is the mass of solute per 100 g of solvent, calculated as (mass_solute / mass_solvent) x 100.
State the solubility in grams of solute per 100 g of solvent at the given temperature and relate it to how temperature changes the value.

worked_examples.question: 36 g of sodium chloride dissolves in 100 g of water at 25 C. What is the solubility?
worked_examples.solution: Solubility = (36 / 100) x 100 = 36 g per 100 g of water.
worked_examples.answer: 36 g per 100 g of water at 25 C.

worked_examples.question: At a certain temperature, 24 g of potassium nitrate dissolves in 80 g of water. Find the solubility.
worked_examples.solution: Solubility = (24 / 80) x 100 = 30 g per 100 g of water.

exercises.question: Define solubility. State two factors that affect the solubility of a solid in a liquid.
40 g of sugar dissolves in 50 g of water at 20 C. Calculate the solubility.

concepts.title: Concentration of Solutions
concepts.definition: Concentration of a solution is the amount of solute present in a given amount of solution or solvent, commonly expressed as a mass percentage.
concepts.formula: concentration (%) = (mass of solute / mass of solution) x 100
concepts.key_idea: Concentration tells how much solute is packed in a solution; mass percentage relates the mass of the solute to the total mass of the solution.
question_patterns: Define concentration of a solution.
Calculate the mass percentage of a solution containing 10 g of salt in 90 g of water.
How is concentration different from solubility?
A solution has 5 g of solute in 100 g of solution. Find its concentration.
Express the concentration of a 15% sugar solution in words.

solution_steps.action: Find the mass of the solution
solution_steps.explain: Add the mass of the solute and the mass of the solvent to get the total mass of the solution.
Concentration (mass %) equals the mass of the solute divided by the mass of the solution, multiplied by 100.
Report the concentration as a percentage and verify it lies between 0 and 100.

worked_examples.question: A solution contains 10 g of salt dissolved in 90 g of water. What is the concentration of the solution?
worked_examples.solution: Mass of solution = 10 + 90 = 100 g. Concentration = (10 / 100) x 100 = 10%.

worked_examples.question: 5 g of sugar is dissolved in 45 g of water. Find the mass percentage concentration.
worked_examples.solution: Mass of solution = 5 + 45 = 50 g. Concentration = (5 / 50) x 100 = 10%.

worked_examples.question: What mass of solute is present in 200 g of a 15% salt solution?
worked_examples.solution: Mass of solute = 15% of 200 g = (15/100) x 200 = 30 g.

exercises.question: Calculate the concentration of a solution made by dissolving 20 g of sugar in 80 g of water.
Distinguish between a dilute and a concentrated solution.

concepts.title: Saturated and Unsaturated Solutions
concepts.definition: A saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve at a given temperature, while an unsaturated solution can dissolve more solute at the same temperature.
concepts.key_idea: At a fixed temperature, a saturated solution is in equilibrium with undissolved solute; adding more solute to an unsaturated solution will dissolve it, but adding to a saturated solution leaves it undissolved.
question_patterns: Differentiate between a saturated and an unsaturated solution.
How can you convert a saturated solution into an unsaturated one?
What happens when more solute is added to a saturated solution at constant temperature?
Explain how heating helps dissolve more solute in a saturated solution.
Describe a simple test to check whether a solution is saturated.

solution_steps.action: Add a small amount of solute
solution_steps.explain: Add a crystal of the same solute to the solution at a constant temperature and observe whether it dissolves.
If the added crystal dissolves, the solution is unsaturated; if it settles at the bottom undissolved, the solution is saturated.
Conclude that heating a saturated solution can make it unsaturated again by increasing the solubility, while cooling an unsaturated solution may saturate it.

worked_examples.question: A student adds more sugar to a sugar solution at 20 C and it does not dissolve. What type of solution is it?
worked_examples.solution: Since no more solute dissolves at the given temperature, the solution has reached its maximum capacity and is saturated.

worked_examples.question: How can a saturated salt solution be made unsaturated without changing the amount of solute?
worked_examples.solution: By heating the solution, the solubility of the salt increases, allowing more solute to dissolve, which makes the solution unsaturated.
worked_examples.answer: Heat the solution to increase solubility.

exercises.question: Define saturated and unsaturated solutions with examples.
State whether the following is saturated or unsaturated: a salt solution in which added salt settles at the bottom.

concepts.title: Properties of Solutions
concepts.definition: A true solution is homogeneous, its particles are too small to be seen, it does not scatter a beam of light, and the solute cannot be separated by simple filtration.
concepts.key_idea: Solutions are stable, homogeneous mixtures with very small solute particles (less than 1 nm) that do not settle out or scatter light (Tyndall effect is absent).
question_patterns: List the characteristic properties of a true solution.
Why does a solution not show the Tyndall effect?
Can the components of a solution be separated by filtration? Explain.
Why is a solution considered stable?
Compare the particle size in a true solution with that in a suspension.

solution_steps.explain: Observe whether the mixture is uniform throughout with no visible particles or layers.
Pass a beam of light through the solution; a true solution will not scatter the light, so the path remains invisible.
Allow the solution to stand and try filtering it; the solute will not settle out and will pass through the filter paper, confirming it is a true solution.

worked_examples.question: A beam of light passed through a liquid is not visible from the side. Is the liquid a true solution?
worked_examples.solution: Absence of the Tyndall effect means the particles are too small to scatter light, which is a property of a true solution.
worked_examples.answer: Yes, it is likely a true solution.

worked_examples.question: Why can salt not be recovered from a salt solution by simple filtration?
worked_examples.solution: In a true solution the solute particles are smaller than the pores of filter paper, so they pass through and cannot be separated by filtration.
worked_examples.answer: Solute particles are too small to be filtered out.

exercises.question: State any three properties of a true solution.
Does a true solution show the Tyndall effect? Give a reason.

concepts.title: Separation of Solutions by Evaporation and Distillation
concepts.definition: The components of a solution can be separated by physical methods such as evaporation, which recovers the solute, and distillation, which collects the solvent by condensing the vapour.
concepts.key_idea: Evaporation separates a volatile solvent from a non-volatile solute, while distillation boils the mixture and condenses the vapour to obtain the pure solvent.
question_patterns: How can you obtain salt from a salt-water solution?
Explain the process of distillation with a labelled description.
Why is evaporation used to separate dyes from ink?
Differentiate between evaporation and distillation.
Which method would you use to obtain pure water from sea water? Why?

solution_steps.explain: Decide whether the goal is to recover the solute (use evaporation) or the solvent (use distillation).
For evaporation, heat the solution until the solvent escapes leaving the solute; for distillation, boil the solution and condense the vapour using a condenser.
Collect the solid residue in evaporation or the condensed liquid in distillation, and verify its purity.

worked_examples.question: How will you obtain common salt from sea water?
worked_examples.solution: Sea water is heated in shallow pans. The water evaporates, leaving behind the solid common salt as residue.

worked_examples.question: A student wants to obtain pure water from an ink-water mixture. Which method should be used?
worked_examples.solution: Distillation is used because the water (solvent) can be boiled off and then condensed to give pure water, leaving the ink behind.

exercises.question: Describe how distillation can be used to obtain pure water from a salt solution.
Which separation method recovers only the solute: evaporation or distillation?
